record.reason: Write B=O_X[T_1,…,T_d]. A finite homogeneous basis e_j of degree a_j gives the degree-preserving isomorphism φ:⊕_j B(−a_j)→L, (b_j)↦Σ_jb_je_j, with inverse the unique homogeneous coordinates. Taking associated sheaves gives ⊕_jO_P(−a_j)≅Proj(L). On D_+(T_i), the degree-zero generators e_j/T_i^{a_j} give explicit local bases and prove finite local freeness. Global freeness is false for an admissible instance: A=k[x,y], J=(x,y), S=A[T_1,T_2]/(yT_1−xT_2), with presentation B(−1)→B→S. Its sheaves are M″=O_{P^1_A}(−1), M′=O. Main491 and native witness488 both print all three names. The governing assumption in2.1 and2.2 is only that f is lissifiable; complete-intersection hypotheses first appear in2.4. Take Y=Spec k, V=V′=Spec B with B=k[x,y], p=id, I=m² for m=(x,y), C=B/I and X=Spec C. Then i′=j=i is the closed immersion defined by m². At the unique point, I/I²=m²/m⁴ has k-dimension3+4=7 (degree2 and degree3 monomials), while C has length3. Thus I/I² cannot be a finite free C-module, whose length would be a multiple of3; a regular immersion would have a finite free conormal module, so these two immersions are not regular. The section j′ is id_X and is regular of codimension0. In general the actual j′ is a section of the smooth p′ and is regular, precisely the source fact used to identify its conormal with relative differentials on478. The short conormal sequence remains justified without regularity of i′ or j: in the affine notation B→B′, C=B/I and J=ker(B′→C), smoothness supplies a B-algebra lift ℓ:B′→B/I² of B′→C through the square-zero quotient B/I²→C. The usual quotient J/J²→K/K², with K=J/IB′, has kernel the image of α; the retraction proves its injectivity, giving exactly2.2.3. Locally free relative differentials of the smooth p′ and the section identify K/K² with j*Ω¹_{V′/V}; the explicit inverse is described by the augmentation calculation on478. This repairs only the false two-immersion assertion and retains the author’s displayed sequences and proof.

source_record.printed_reading: C has integral k-algebras and flat homomorphisms; F commutes filtered inductive limits; the later assertions claim injectivity, torsion kernel and bijectivity

source_record.change: Preserve the author’s body in both layers; record the established source error and the unresolved emendation in the apparatus.
source_record.reason: Direct main comparison and witnesses601–603 establish the exact source hypotheses. In7.18.1 C consists of integral k-algebras with flat homomorphisms and F:C→Ens commutes filtered inductive limits. In7.18.2 the printed cases are(a) k separably closed and K/k separable,(b) k infinite and K/k pure; its conclusion is injectivity. The proof uses F(A→k), but evaluation k[t]→k at t=0 is not flat: tensoring the injective multiplication-by-t map on k[t] gives the zero map on nonzero k. Here is a concrete counterexample on exactly the printed category. Fix algebraically closed k and define G(A)=Z when Frac(A)/k is algebraic and G(A)=0 otherwise. Every flat map of nonzero domains A→B is injective: for nonzero a in A, flatness preserves the injection A --a→ A after tensoring with B; if a mapped to0, the resulting zero map B→B would be injective, forcing B=0. Hence Frac(A) injects into Frac(B), so transcendence over k cannot disappear. Define G on arrows by identity when both values are Z and by the unique map whenever the target is0. There is no arrow from the transcendental case to the algebraic case; these maps compose exactly, so G is a functor. A filtered diagram of these injections has an integral colimit. Every fraction in the colimit comes from a stage. If every stage fraction field is algebraic over k, every such fraction is algebraic, so G(colim A_i)=Z=colim G(A_i). If some stage contains a transcendental element, it remains transcendental in all later stages; the stages receiving that stage are cofinal and G is0 there, so both sides are0. Thus G commutes the required filtered limits. Now K=k(t) satisfies both printed cases(a) and(b), but G(k)→G(K) is Z→0, which is not injective. For the exact set-valued version one may replace Z and0 by a fixed two-element set and a singleton, with the same identity/collapse maps and the same colimit calculation. In7.18.3 the additional norm hypothesis is that F(k)→F(k′)→F(k) is multiplication by[k′:k] for each finite extension k′/k. Since k is algebraically closed, every such extension has degree1, and choosing the identity norm for G satisfies this hypothesis. Its kernel Z for K=k(t) is not torsion, and its map is not injective, refuting both printed conclusions(i),(ii) on592. Finally7.18.4 assumes surjectivity for the coordinate ring A of every nonempty affine open U⊂A_k^n. For n>0, Frac(A)=k(T_1,…,T_n), so G(k)→G(A) is Z→0 and is surjective; for n=0 it is id_Z. Thus the added assumption holds, k is infinite, and the norm hypothesis also holds, yet Z→0 is not bijective. This refutes its final bijectivity conclusion, not its surjectivity conclusion. The specific K_• functor in7.18.5 has additional finite-Tor pullbacks (the printed citation IV2.12), not supplied for arbitrary F in7.18.1; the present counterexample does not refute those specific K_• conclusions. No corrected general theorem or new hypothesis is inserted.
